propositions.text: Applicants seek judicial review of RAD decision under section 72 of IRPA.
propositions.quote: The Applicants seek the judicial review of the decision made by the Refugee Appeal Division [RAD]. The judicial review is made under section 72 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA]

propositions.text: The judicial review concerns RAD decision affirming RPD decision that Applicants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: and concerns the appeal decision which affirmed the decision of the Refugee Protection Division [RPD] finding that the Applicants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection (sections 96 and 97 of IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: Applicants seek judicial review of RAD decision affirming RPD finding Applicants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.

propositions.text: RPD and RAD concluded Principal Applicant's credibility was determinative for all Applicants.
propositions.quote: Both the RPD and the RAD concluded that the credibility of the Principal Applicant, Sabib Singh, was the determinative issue for all four of the Applicants.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant's testimony changed during RPD hearing and evolved on appeal with new evidence and allegations.
propositions.quote: During the RPD hearing, the Principal Applicant’s testimony changed when asked about the same events more than once. On appeal, his narrative evolved again as he sought to introduce new evidence and allegations.

paragraphs.summary: RPD and RAD found Principal Applicant's credibility determinative; his testimony changed during RPD hearing and evolved on appeal.

propositions.text: RAD's decision was reasonable and properly considered credibility and new evidence under IRPA and case law.
propositions.quote: I find that the RAD’s decision was reasonable. The RAD appropriately made findings on the Principal Applicant’s credibility and considered whether to admit new evidence in accordance with the IRPA and established case law.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review will be dismissed.
propositions.quote: Therefore, this application will be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD decision reasonable and dismisses judicial review application.

propositions.text: Applicants are Indian Sikh family; Principal Applicant was a farmer owning a dairy farm in Karnal.
propositions.quote: The Applicants are a family of Indian nationality and Sikh faith. The Principal Applicant was a farmer who owned a dairy farm in the city of Karnal.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant fears persecution from Indian police acting for Ms. Davinder Kaur (Gogi).
propositions.quote: He alleges that he fears persecution from the Indian police acting on behalf of Ms. Davinder Kaur (“Gogi”).

propositions.text: Gogi is sister of Principal Applicant’s childhood best friend, Jatinder Singh, and connected to army and ruling party.
propositions.quote: Gogi is the sister of the Principal Applicant’s childhood best friend, Jatinder Singh. The Principal Applicant asserts that Gogi and her husband’s family are well-connected members of the army and India’s ruling party.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants are Indian Sikh family; Principal Applicant fears persecution from police acting for Gogi, connected to army and ruling party.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant's fear stems from four incidents over two decades: 2001, 2010, 2017, and post-arrival in Canada.
propositions.quote: The Principal Applicant’s fear of persecution stems from four incidents that occurred over a period of two decades.

propositions.text: 2001 incident: Principal Applicant angered Gogi over adoption plan of Jatinder’s son.
propositions.quote: The first incident happened in 2001, when the Principal Applicant angered Gogi by being critical of her plan to adopt her brother (Jatinder)’s son.

propositions.text: 2010 incident: Gogi threatened to kill Principal Applicant after property dispute.
propositions.quote: Next, in 2010, Gogi allegedly threatened to kill the Principal Applicant after he again interfered in her family affairs, this time concerning the division of property between Gogi and her brother.

propositions.text: 2017 incident: Gogi bribed police to torture and falsely charge Principal Applicant over Sikh temple construction.
propositions.quote: Third, the Principal Applicant alleges that in 2017, Gogi resorted to bribing local police officials to subject him to torture and falsely implicate him in criminal charges related to his role in the construction of a Sikh temple.

propositions.text: Post-arrival incident: Police issued 'wanted notice' served on friend in 2019 after Applicants arrived in Canada.
propositions.quote: The final incident arose after the Applicants’ arrival in Canada but prior to the RPD hearing. ... local police in India issued a “wanted notice” of the Principal Applicant and served it on his friend, Neelam Notna, on September 20, 2019.

propositions.text: Applicants arrived in Canada June 25, 2017, and sought refugee protection December 28, 2017.
propositions.quote: He and his family arrived in Canada on June 25, 2017. The Applicants sought refugee protection on December 28, 2017.

paragraphs.summary: Principal Applicant's fear arises from four incidents (2001, 2010, 2017, post-arrival); Applicants arrived Canada June 2017, claimed refugee December 2017.

propositions.text: Significant time gaps exist between alleged incidents, important to assessment.
propositions.quote: there are significant time gaps between the alleged incidents that are said to give rise to the justification for seeking refugee status in Canada.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant testified about 'minor incidents' during gaps but did not document them in BOC or amendments.
propositions.quote: he chose not to document them on his Basis of Claim form (BOC) nor in subsequent amendments to his BOC.

propositions.text: During RPD hearing, Principal Applicant could not answer basic questions about nature and content of incidents during gaps.
propositions.quote: During the RPD hearing, the Principal Applicant was not able to answer basic questions when prompted to provide further information regarding the nature and content of these incidents on the time gaps.

paragraphs.summary: Significant time gaps between incidents; Principal Applicant described minor incidents but did not document them and could not explain details at RPD hearing.

propositions.text: 2001 incident: Principal Applicant alleges Jatinder gave son for adoption to Gogi; he upset Gogi by opposing adoption.
propositions.quote: The Principal Applicant alleges that his childhood friend Jatinder gave up his son Akashdeep for adoption to his sister Gogi. The Principal Applicant claims that he upset Gogi by trying to convince Jatinder not to go through with the adoption.

propositions.text: Gogi has held a grudge against Principal Applicant since 2001 incident.
propositions.quote: According to him, Gogi has held a grudge against him since this incident.

paragraphs.summary: Principal Applicant alleges 2001 adoption dispute upset Gogi, who has held a grudge since.

propositions.text: No information provided about events from 2001 to 2010.
propositions.quote: The Principal Applicant provides no information about any event arising over the next nine years (i.e. from 2001 to 2010).

propositions.text: 2010 incident: Gogi sought to reverse adoption after family argument; Principal Applicant involved in verbal altercation and received death threat.
propositions.quote: At some point in 2010, Gogi allegedly sought to reverse the adoption of her brother Jatinder’s son following an argument she had with him and their father. ... he claims he received a death threat.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant began fearing for his life in 2010.
propositions.quote: Based on the Principal Applicant’s testimony, he began fearing for his life at that time.

paragraphs.summary: No events described 2001-2010; 2010 incident involved adoption reversal dispute, death threat, and start of fear for life.

propositions.text: RPD sought details about 2010-2017 period; Principal Applicant said only 'small incidents' occurred.
propositions.quote: During the RPD hearing, it sought to gain a better understanding of the intervening years from 2010 to 2017, which is when the next incident allegedly occurred. The Principal Applicant stated that only “small incidents” happened over this period.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant claimed in 2010 he was 'forced to save his life' after being followed; in 2014 saw another follower; no details given.
propositions.quote: The Principal Applicant also stated that in 2014, he saw another individual follow him. No details were forthcoming.

propositions.text: RPD questioned why these incidents were not mentioned in BOC or amendments; Principal Applicant said they were 'small incidents' not worth mentioning.
propositions.quote: The RPD member questioned why the Principal Applicant had not mentioned these events on his BOC nor its subsequent amendments. The Principal Applicant stated as follows: “For me, there was small incidents that happened on me.

paragraphs.summary: RPD questioned 2010-2017 'small incidents' not in BOC; Principal Applicant said only major incidents were reported.

propositions.text: RPD identified inconsistencies in residency and travel history: BOC says Karnal 2007-2016; visa says Karnal since 2005; testimony says moved to Karnal in 2014.
propositions.quote: On Schedule A of his Generic Application Form, the Principal Applicant indicated that he had lived and worked in the city of Karnal from 2007 to 2016. However, his temporary visa application specified that he worked in Karnal since 2005. Moreover, during the hearing, the Principal Applicant testified that he had relocated his family from the village of Peont to Karnal in 2014.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant explained inconsistencies by interpreter error and mother's advice to move to Karnal after 'small incidents'.
propositions.quote: When given the opportunity to explain the apparent contradictions, the Principal Applicant first stated that there may have been an error on the part of the interpreter, and then explained that his mother was living in Karnal and had advised him to move there following the two “small incidents” in 2010 and 2014 respectively.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found inconsistencies in residency dates; Principal Applicant attributed to interpreter error and mother's advice after incidents.

propositions.text: Applicants traveled to France and Eastern Europe in 2016 for tourism.
propositions.quote: The Applicants’ passports reveal that they traveled for tourism purposes to France and Eastern Europe in 2016.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant said he did not claim asylum during trips because no physical attack yet and friend assured situation would deescalate.
propositions.quote: When asked why he had not claimed asylum over the course of these touristic trips, the Principal Applicant responded that since he had not yet been physically attacked, he did not feel the need to seek asylum abroad. He added that he was living very cautiously in India and his friend Jatinder had assured him that the situation with Gogi would deescalate.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants traveled to Europe in 2016; Principal Applicant said no asylum claim as no physical attack and friend assured deescalation.

propositions.text: Applicants applied for temporary resident visas to visit Canada on April 9, 2017.
propositions.quote: On April 9, 2017, the Applicants applied for temporary resident visas to visit Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants applied for temporary resident visas to Canada on April 9, 2017.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant involved in Sikh temple construction in Manchuri near Karnal; had no links to village.
propositions.quote: It is around this time that the Principal Applicant says he got involved in building a Sikh temple (Gurdwara) in the village of Manchuri, near the city of Karnal. The RPD identified that the Principal Applicant had no links to the village of Manchuri

propositions.text: Principal Applicant did not explain importance of temple or his specific role; said he collected money and had supervisory role.
propositions.quote: He did not respond to the question. Instead, he replied that the land had previously belonged to a Sikh person. He was also asked three times to explain specifically what his role was in the construction of the temple. The Principal Applicant ended up stating that he and others “collected money” and that he had a supervisory role.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant said Sikh community was poor and he was raising his voice for Sikhs without details.
propositions.quote: He reiterated that the state of the Sikh community in his area was very poor and that he was “raising [his] voice” for the Sikhs without providing further details.

paragraphs.summary: Principal Applicant involved in Sikh temple construction in Manchuri; gave vague explanations of role and community advocacy.

propositions.text: BOC states local MLA neglected temple construction causing confrontation on April 28, 2017.
propositions.quote: According to the Principal Applicant's BOC, a local MLA intentionally neglected and delayed the construction of the temple, leading to a confrontation on April 28, 2017.

propositions.text: Amended BOC alleges Principal Applicant was physically obstructed by 15-20 individuals at construction site on April 28, 2017.
propositions.quote: In a subsequent amendment to his BOC, the Principal Applicant alleges that on that day, he attempted to access the construction site to begin building. However, when he arrived, he was met by 15-20 individuals and was physically obstructed from accessing the site.

propositions.text: During hearing, Principal Applicant changed narrative to say Gogi was present and invited MLA to obstruct him.
propositions.quote: During the hearing, the Principal Applicant changed his narrative. He stated for the first time that Gogi was present and it was she who had invited the MLA to obstruct his passage.

propositions.text: RPD asked why Gogi's presence was omitted in original and amended BOC; Principal Applicant did not answer.
propositions.quote: The RPD asked the Principal Applicant three times why he had omitted the fact that Gogi was present on the Sikh temple’s construction site in his original and later amended BOC form. Again, the Principal Applicant did not answer the question.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant said Gogi was on sidelines while others were forefront at construction site.
propositions.quote: He responded that Gogi was on the sidelines whereas members of the “Kasha Clan” and the MLA were in the forefront of the construction site.

paragraphs.summary: BOC alleges April 28, 2017 confrontation at temple site; Principal Applicant changed story to include Gogi's presence but did not explain omission.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant claims he was tortured by police at station on April 28, 2017, under Gogi's orders.
propositions.quote: That same day, the Principal Applicant attended a nearby police station to file a complaint against the MLA. It is there that he claims he was “tortured” by the local police acting under Gogi’s orders.

propositions.text: He was detained overnight, beaten with belts and kicked, questioned about Sikh terrorists and told to stop interfering in family matters.
propositions.quote: he was detained over night in police custody and was hit with belts and kicked in the stomach and on the back for over an hour. The officers allegedly demanded information concerning Sikh terrorists, questioned him regarding his interest in the Manchuri village and advised him to stop getting involved in the family matters of Gogi and Jatinder.

paragraphs.summary: Principal Applicant alleges police tortured him on April 28, 2017, beating and questioning him under Gogi's orders.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant tendered medical report showing leg fracture with implanted rod moved due to torture in 2017.
propositions.quote: the Principal Applicant was asked questions related to a medical report he tendered as evidence that was issued by the Metro-Medic Clinic in Montreal on January 7, 2019. The Principal Applicant explained that he had fractured his leg in the past resulting in him receiving an implanted rod. He went on to explain that due to the torture he sustained at the hands of the police on April 28, 2017, the rod had moved and he required additional care in Montreal for his leg.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant did not mention leg injury earlier; said he only became aware of severity after arriving in Montreal.
propositions.quote: When asked why he did not mention hurting his leg earlier when questioned about injuries related to the torture incident, the Principal Applicant responded that he only became aware of the severity of his injuries after arriving in Montreal.

paragraphs.summary: Principal Applicant submitted medical report of leg injury from 2017 torture; said he only realized severity after arriving in Montreal.

propositions.text: Applicants obtained temporary resident visas May 2, 2017, less than a week after April 27-28 events.
propositions.quote: Having applied for visas on April 9, 2017, the Applicants obtained temporary resident visas to visit Canada on May 2, 2017, less than one week after the events of April 27 and 28.

propositions.text: Applicants arrived in Canada June 25, 2017, and sought refugee protection six months later on December 28, 2017.
propositions.quote: They arrived in Canada on June 25, 2017, and sought refugee protection six months later on December 28, 2017.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants got visas May 2, 2017, arrived June 25, 2017, and claimed refugee protection December 28, 2017.

propositions.text: In amended BOC, Principal Applicant asserted police issued 'wanted notice' served on friend in 2019 after leaving India.
propositions.quote: In a subsequent amendment to his BOC, the Principal Applicant asserted that police had issued a “wanted notice” in his name and served it on his friend Neelam Notna on September 20, 2019, more than two years after having left India.

propositions.text: RPD found photograph on 'wanted notice' identical to one taken in Montreal in December 2017, undermining claim.
propositions.quote: The RPD identified blatant similarities between this photograph and the one submitted with his refugee protection claim forms in December 2017. The RPD noted that the original photograph associated with his protection claim stated it was taken at a photography shop in Montreal on December 10, 2017.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant said he did not know where police got photo and must have worn same clothes when arrested in April 2017.
propositions.quote: When asked about the identical nature of both photos, the Principal Applicant responded that he did not know where the police had found the photograph and that he must have been wearing the same clothes on April 28, 2017, when he was arrested.

paragraphs.summary: Principal Applicant claimed police issued 'wanted notice' in 2019; RPD found photo identical to one taken in Montreal in 2017, undermining claim.

propositions.text: RPD denied refugee claim due to Principal Applicant's credibility deficiencies.
propositions.quote: The RPD denied the Applicants’ refugee protection claim for the deficiencies of the Principal Applicant’s credibility.

propositions.text: RPD summarized credibility issues: 'warrant notice' contradicted by evidence; serving procedures inconsistent; identical photos unexplained; omission of Gogi's presence unexplained; unsatisfactory injury explanation; travel undermined fear claim; 2014 move claim lacked credibility.
propositions.quote: The series of inconsistencies and contradictions the RPD found regarding the credibility of the Principal Applicant are summarized as follows: The reliance on a “warrant notice” issued by a local police station to support the Principal Applicant’s claim of being pursued by the police acting under Gogi’s orders was contradicted by objective evidence that such documents are issued by courts in India. His allegation that he received the “wanted notice” after it was served on his friend Neelam Notna upon leaving India goes against objective evidence of how documents are served in India. The Principal Applicant failed to provide an adequate explanation for why the photograph in his refugee protection claim was the same as the one taken at the police station on April 28, 2017. The Principal Applicant did not provide a reasonable explanation for why he had failed to mention that Gogi was present on the Sikh temple’s construction site until he was questioned about it during the hearing. His explanation for omitting the fact that he suffered a leg fracture and that the rod implanted in his leg was displaced as a result of the “torture” was not satisfactory. In particular, it contradicted his earlier testimony concerning the injuries he sustained. The Applicants’ travels to France and Eastern Europe in 2016 undermined their credibility given the Principal Applicant’s contention that he began fearing for his life in 2010. Finally, the allegation that an incident in 2014 prompted the Principal Applicant to move to Karnal out of a concern for his safety lacked credibility because it was only raised during his testimony and contradicted his BOC which indicated that he had lived in Karnal since 2005.

paragraphs.summary: RPD denied claim due to multiple credibility deficiencies including contradictory evidence, unexplained omissions, and inconsistent travel and residency claims.

propositions.text: Applicants appealed RPD decision on grounds of unfair hearing and erroneous credibility assessment.
propositions.quote: The Applicants appealed the RPD’s decision on two grounds. First, the Applicants argued that they did not have a fair hearing before the RPD because the panel failed to consider the Principal Applicant’s evidence or listen to his explanations. Second, it was contended that the RPD erred in its assessment of the Principal Applicant’s credibility.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants appealed RPD decision alleging unfair hearing and errors in credibility assessment.

propositions.text: The decision under review is that of the Refugee Appeal Division.
propositions.quote: The decision under review is that of the Refugee Appeal Division.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the decision under review is that of the Refugee Appeal Division.

propositions.text: Applicants attached eight additional exhibits to the Principal Applicant's affidavit as new evidence before the RAD.
propositions.quote: To forward their argument on appeal before the RAD on the Principal Applicant’s credibility, the Applicants attached eight additional exhibits to his affidavit as new evidence

propositions.text: Section 110(4) IRPA governs admissibility of new evidence on appeal before the RAD.
propositions.quote: Section 110(4), which governs the admissibility of new evidence on appeal before the RAD, provides the following: Evidence that may be presented Éléments de preuve admissibles (4) On appeal, the person who is the subject of the appeal may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Applicants attached eight new exhibits and cites section 110(4) IRPA governing new evidence admissibility before the RAD.

propositions.text: The new evidence consists of eight exhibits: five affidavits, a letter, a medical certificate, and an excerpt from Indian Code of Criminal Procedure.
propositions.quote: The new evidence consisted of five undated affidavits signed by the Applicants’ neighbours (Exhibits A-E), an undated letter written by Jatinder Singh’s son (Exhibit F), a medical certificate concerning Jatinder Singh dated February 9, 2021 (Exhibit G), as well as an excerpt from the Indian Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Exhibit H).

propositions.text: Summaries of each exhibit describe affidavits warning against return to India, letter about shooting, medical certificate, and legal excerpt.
propositions.quote: I summarize the new evidence as follows: Exhibit A: An affidavit accompanied with a letter signed by Neelam Notna... Exhibit H: An excerpt from the Indian Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

paragraphs.summary: The court summarizes the eight new exhibits including affidavits, letter, medical certificate, and legal excerpt.

propositions.text: Three affidavits (Exhibits C, D, E) are identical except for names, addresses, and signatures.
propositions.quote: It is important to note that three of the affidavits (Exhibits C, D and E) are identical, save for the addresses, signature and names appearing on the three affidavits.

propositions.text: Example affidavit text warns against return to India due to police search and alleges illegal torture linked to Gogi.
propositions.quote: For example, Savinder Kaur’s affidavit states: 1. 1 have known to sahib Singh personally since 2014... Police often come to his neighbors including me (Savinder Kaur) for assigning about him.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes three affidavits are identical except for names and gives an example affidavit warning against return to India.

propositions.text: The RAD considered whether to admit the eight exhibits as new evidence applying criteria from FCA decisions Singh and Raza.
propositions.quote: At the outset, the RAD considered whether to admit the eight exhibits introduced by the Applicants as new evidence. The RAD applied the criteria established by two Federal Court of Appeal decisions (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Singh, 2016 FCA 96...

propositions.text: The RAD admitted only the Indian Criminal Code excerpt (Exhibit H) and did not hold an oral hearing as it was not central.
propositions.quote: The RAD ruled that it would only admit the excerpt from the Indian Criminal Code (Exhibit H). Since this evidence was not central to its decision, the RAD did not find cause to hold an oral hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD applied FCA criteria and admitted only the Indian Criminal Code excerpt, declining an oral hearing as it was not central.

propositions.text: The RAD did not admit Exhibits A to G due to lack of credibility, reliability, or reasonable availability before claim rejection.
propositions.quote: The RAD did not admit the remaining seven exhibits (Exhibits A to G) on the basis that they lacked credibility, reliability, or were reasonably available before the rejection of the Applicants’ claim under subsection 110(4) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD excluded Exhibits A to G for lacking credibility, reliability, or reasonable availability before claim rejection.

propositions.text: The RAD found credibility of Exhibits A to E undermined by grammatical and spelling errors in notary seals.
propositions.quote: The credibility of the first five exhibits (Exhibits A to E)... were undermined in two ways. First, by the presence of a grammatical and a spelling error in the notary’s official wet seal.

propositions.text: The RAD also noted none of these documents were dated.
propositions.quote: Second, none of these documents were dated.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found Exhibits A to E lacked credibility due to notary seal errors and absence of dates.

propositions.text: Admissibility under s.110(4) IRPA requires compliance with explicit provision and five implied conditions from Singh/Raza: credibility, relevance, newness, materiality, express statutory conditions.
propositions.quote: In Singh, the Federal Court of Appeal held that a determination of the admissibility of evidence under section 110(4) must always ensure compliance with the explicit requirements of the provision, but can also be guided by the five “implied” conditions of admissibility identified by Justice Sharlow in Raza (Singh, para 38). These are: credibility, relevance, newness, materiality, and express statutory conditions.

propositions.text: The RAD noted even if Exhibits A to E were dated and error-free, they still did not meet s.110(4) criteria.
propositions.quote: The RAD noted that in any event (i.e. even if five exhibits were dated and did not contain spelling and grammatical errors on the seal), the new evidence did not meet the criteria required under subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, as interpreted under the Singh/Raza framework.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD applied Singh/Raza criteria and found Exhibits A to E would still fail admissibility under s.110(4) IRPA.

propositions.text: RAD found Exhibit A failed all Singh/Raza criteria but gave no detailed explanation.
propositions.quote: The RAD held that Exhibit A did not meet any of the Singh/Raza criteria, but it did not provide a fuller explanation for why the criteria were not met (RAD decision, para 9, 14).

propositions.text: RAD did not admit Exhibits B to F because events described were not shown to arise after claim rejection or were reasonably available before RPD.
propositions.quote: The RAD did not admit the next five exhibits (Exhibits B to F) because it could not ascertain whether the events described in the documents had occurred after the Applicants’ claims were rejected by the RPD or why steps taken to secure such evidence could not have been taken with appropriate diligence.

propositions.text: RAD found evidence could reasonably have been expected to be presented before RPD, so did not meet s.110(4) requirements.
propositions.quote: Moreover, that evidence could reasonably have been expected to have been presented before the RPD. As such, the evidence could not meet the requirements of s. 110(4).

paragraphs.summary: The RAD rejected Exhibits A to F for failing Singh/Raza criteria and being reasonably available before RPD.

propositions.text: Exhibit G medical certificate dated before claim rejection was inadmissible as it could have been presented to RPD.
propositions.quote: The certificate was issued before the claim was rejected by the RPD. The RAD held this was inadmissible on the basis that it could have reasonably been put before the RPD...

propositions.text: Therefore, Exhibit G did not meet s.110(4) criteria for new evidence.
propositions.quote: ...and therefore did not meet the criteria under subsection 110(4) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD excluded Exhibit G medical certificate as it was issued before claim rejection and could have been presented to RPD.

propositions.text: RAD declined to consider four new allegations in Principal Applicant’s affidavit as they arose before RPD hearing.
propositions.quote: The RAD also declined to consider four new allegations presented by the Principal Applicant in his affidavit on the basis that they arose before the RPD hearing.

propositions.text: The four allegations involved Gogi's family connections, a 2014 car incident, and a wanted notice photograph.
propositions.quote: The allegations were as follows: Gogi's husband and extended family are in the Indian army... The photograph on a wanted notice issued by the Indian police was likely obtained by the police searching for the Principal Applicant through his social media accounts.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD declined to consider four new allegations as they arose before the RPD hearing.

propositions.text: RAD admitted only one exhibit and then considered the merits, finding Applicants had a fair hearing and RPD did not err on credibility.
propositions.quote: After making the determination that only one of the eight exhibits should be admitted into evidence, the RAD moved on to consider the merits of the appeal. It held that the Applicants had received a fair hearing and the RPD did not err in its assessment of the Principal Applicant’s credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD admitted one exhibit, found Applicants had a fair hearing, and upheld RPD's credibility assessment.

propositions.text: RAD found no error in procedural fairness: Applicants had opportunity to present evidence, interpreter, counsel, submissions, and reasons.
propositions.quote: In this case, the appellants had the opportunity to present their evidence to the RPD at the hearing... The appellants benefited from having an interpreter and were represented by counsel before the RPD... When it rendered its decision rejecting the refugee protection claim, the RPD gave the appellants its reasons.

propositions.text: Applicants did not explain how RPD failed to deliver a fair hearing.
propositions.quote: With respect to the first issue, the RAD noted that the Applicants had not explained how the RPD had failed to deliver a fair hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found no procedural fairness error and noted Applicants did not explain any failure by RPD.

propositions.text: RAD found no reasonable apprehension of bias under Committee for Justice and Liberty test.
propositions.quote: Nor did the RAD find that the Applicants had established the existence of a reasonable apprehension of bias pursuant to the test in Committee for Justice and Liberty et al v National Energy Board et al., [1978) 1 SCR 369.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found no reasonable apprehension of bias under the applicable test.

propositions.text: RAD made adverse credibility findings due to inconsistencies in Principal Applicant’s testimony and delays in leaving India.
propositions.quote: The RAD made an adverse credibility finding from how the Principal Applicant’s testimony about the threats and incidents allegedly involving Gogi did not match the information set out in his BOC or its amendments...

propositions.text: Credibility undermined by delay in leaving India despite death threat and tourism travel in 2016.
propositions.quote: The Principal Applicant’s credibility was further undermined by his decision not to leave India until 2017, despite claiming that he had received a death threat in 2010 and travelled abroad for tourism purposes in 2016.

propositions.text: Credibility issues with testimony about Sikh temple construction and omissions about torture incidents.
propositions.quote: The RAD also found credibility issues with the Principal Applicant’s testimony concerning his involvement with the construction of the Sikh temple and omissions related to the alleged incidents of torture on April 28, 2017.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant initially said MLA prevented construction; later said Gogi was present and brought MLA.
propositions.quote: In particular, the Principal Applicant had initially testified that an MLA accompanied by 15 to 20 people prevented him from starting construction of the temple. Later during his testimony, the Principal Applicant stated that Gogi was present at the construction site that day and had brought the MLA.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found multiple credibility issues with the Principal Applicant’s testimony and delays in leaving India.

propositions.text: RAD upheld RPD’s finding to give no weight to wanted notice due to unreliable photograph origin.
propositions.quote: Finally, the RAD upheld the RPD’s finding that no weight should be given to a wanted notice that the Principal Applicant claimed was issued by Indian police.

propositions.text: Photograph on wanted notice was taken in Montreal in 2017, undermining reliability and credibility.
propositions.quote: The wanted notice featured the same photograph of the Principal Applicant that he had submitted with his refugee protection claim form. This photograph was taken at a photography shop, on Jean-Talon Avenue in Montreal, on December 20, 2017.

propositions.text: Without explanation for photograph possession, wanted notice was unreliable and undermined credibility overall.
propositions.quote: The RAD held that absent a satisfactory explanation for how this photograph came to be in the possession of the Indian police, the wanted notice was not a reliable document and the anomaly undermined the Principal Applicant’s credibility overall.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD upheld RPD’s rejection of the wanted notice due to unreliable photograph and credibility concerns.

propositions.text: Applicants seek judicial review and remittal, arguing RAD’s refusal to admit new evidence was unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The Applicants ask the Court to grant their judicial review application and remit the matter to another decision maker. Their central argument is that the RAD’s refusal to admit new evidence was unreasonable.

propositions.text: Applicants argue admitted new evidence would establish ongoing threat from Gogi and Indian state.
propositions.quote: The Applicants argue that had this new evidence been admitted, they would have necessarily established an ongoing threat of danger faced by the Applicants from the agent of persecution (Gogi) and the Indian state.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue RAD unreasonably refused new evidence which would show ongoing threat from Gogi and Indian state.

propositions.text: Applicants rely on cases that minor typographical errors should not discredit legitimate documents.
propositions.quote: The Applicants rely on several cases that stand for the proposition that superficial or minor typographical errors in grammar and spelling ought not to be used as a scapegoat to otherwise discredit legitimate documents.

propositions.text: Applicants cite Ali, Ayeni, and Enamejewa cases to argue spelling and grammatical errors were minor typographical errors.
propositions.quote: In Ali v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 814 [Ali] at paragraph 27... Ayeni v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 1202... Enamejewa v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 315 at para 29...

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue minor typographical errors should not discredit documents, citing Ali, Ayeni, and Enamejewa cases.

propositions.text: Applicants’ counsel clarified that even if RAD’s refusal to admit evidence was reasonable, the overall credibility assessment was unreasonable.
propositions.quote: During the hearing, counsel to the Applicants clarified that even if the Court finds that it was reasonable for the RAD not to admit the new evidence, the RAD’s assessment of the Principal Applicant’s credibility was unreasonable as a whole.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue RAD’s overall credibility assessment was unreasonable even if refusal to admit evidence was reasonable.

propositions.text: Respondent seeks dismissal of judicial review, arguing RAD decision was reasonable.
propositions.quote: The Respondent seeks the dismissal of this application for judicial review on the basis that the decision of the RAD was reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues RAD decision was reasonable and seeks dismissal of judicial review application.

propositions.text: RAD reasonably rejected affidavits and letters due to undated documents and significant errors on official notary seal
propositions.quote: The Respondent argues that the RAD reasonably rejected the admission of the affidavits and letters (Exhibits A to E) because these documents were not dated and the grammatical and the spelling error found on an official wet seal of an Indian Notary is no minor typographical error.

propositions.text: Respondent relies on Mohamed v Canada to support RAD's adverse inference on identity documents with errors
propositions.quote: On the latter argument, the Respondent refers the Court’s attention to Mohamed v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 55, where Justice Bell was asked to determine whether it was reasonable for the RAD to draw adverse inferences against a claimant’s ability to establish his identity based on errors in government and educational documents.

propositions.text: Mohamed v Canada found RAD reasonably considered inconsistencies and spelling mistakes on official documents to dismiss judicial review
propositions.quote: I am satisfied the issues raised surrounding those documents are sufficient, in and of themselves, to dismiss this application for judicial review. Continued use of the name “Somali Democratic Republic” in official documents... It was reasonably open for the RAD to find that the use of dated stamps cast doubt on the genuineness of these documents.

propositions.text: Mohamed v Canada distinguished Oranye on spelling mistakes in official documents versus personal affidavits
propositions.quote: While the Applicant relies on Oranye to argue that the presence of spelling mistakes in a document is insufficient to justify a finding of fraud, that case is distinguishable. In Oranye, this Court was concerned about the RAD’s treatment of spelling errors in a personal affidavit. Here, the RAD addressed spelling mistakes on government stamps placed on allegedly official documents.

propositions.text: Azenabor confirmed RAD's reasonable reliance on document issues including font differences and typographical errors in official documents
propositions.quote: In Azenabor v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 1160 [“Azenabor”], this Court stated: [31] Again, I find the RAD’s reliance on these issues as one element of its assessment of the documents to be reasonable. The RAD raised a concern about one of the affidavits...

propositions.text: Typographical errors in official document letterhead raise greater concerns than minor clerical errors in text
propositions.quote: With respect to the typographical errors, there is a difference in my view between a clerical error in the body of a document and material errors in the printed portions of what is contended to be an official corporate identity card. One might, for example, distinguish between a typographical error appearing in this paragraph of this decision, and a misspelling of the words “Federal Court” in the letterhead of the Court: Ali v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 814 at para 31.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues RAD reasonably rejected undated affidavits with errors, relying on Mohamed and Azenabor cases distinguishing official document errors from minor typos.

propositions.text: RAD reasonably refused to admit new evidence about gunshot wound as it was available before RPD hearing
propositions.quote: The Respondent also argues that the RAD reasonably refused to admit new evidence related to the gunshot wound allegedly suffered by the Principal Applicant’s friend Jatinder Singh... since the information was available prior to the RPD hearing, the RAD’s decision to reject their admissibility was reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues RAD reasonably refused new evidence on gunshot wound as it was available before RPD hearing.

propositions.text: Evidence has little probative value; RAD's concerns about Applicants' lack of credibility are main hurdle
propositions.quote: In any event, the Respondent argues that the substance of the evidence at issue has little probative value. The Respondent relies on the RAD’s concerns regarding the Applicants’ lack of credibility as being the main hurdle to the Applicants’ claim for refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues evidence has little probative value; RAD's credibility concerns are main hurdle to claim.

propositions.text: Standard of review is reasonableness per Vavilov, requiring justification, transparency, and intelligibility
propositions.quote: The parties submit, and I agree, that the standard for reviewing this application is reasonableness, as established by the Supreme Court in Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov... A reasonable decision bears the hallmarks that are justification, transparency, and intelligibility, and the decision is justified in light of the relevant legal and factual constraints (para 99).

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees standard of review is reasonableness per Vavilov requiring justification, transparency, and intelligibility.

propositions.text: Issue: Did RAD reasonably refuse Applicants’ evidence on appeal and was RAD’s decision reasonable even if evidence inadmissible?
propositions.quote: The parties also agree on the issues, which can be framed as follows: Did the RAD reasonably refuse to accept the Applicants’ evidence submitted on appeal? Even if the new evidence is not admissible, was the RAD’s decision reasonable?

paragraphs.summary: Court frames issue whether RAD reasonably refused evidence and whether decision was reasonable even if evidence inadmissible.

propositions.text: Reasons must justify and explain outcomes to ensure transparency and intelligibility per Vavilov
propositions.quote: Reasons must justify and explain how outcomes are reached, as stated in Vavilov, to ensure transparency and intelligibility to those affected (Vavilov, para 95). The rationale for the decision is as important as the outcome itself (Vavilov, para 96).

propositions.text: Defective justifications fail transparency standard; reasons required for key elements especially with significant personal impact
propositions.quote: Defective justifications fail to meet the transparency and intelligibility standard, although minor issues may not be fatal. However, if reasons are required for a key element of the decision, they must be provided (Vavilov, para 133). Decisions with significant personal impact or potential harm require reasons that reflect the stakes (Vavilov, para 133).

paragraphs.summary: Court states reasons must justify outcomes for transparency per Vavilov; defective reasons fail standard especially for key elements.

propositions.text: Reviewing courts must respect tribunal's decision, not substitute own reasons, but review remains robust
propositions.quote: Reviewing courts ensure understanding of the decision maker's reasoning but should not provide their own reasons. They operate from the starting point of the principle of restraint and “adopt an appropriate posture of respect” (Vavilov, paras 13-14, 75). A reviewing court does not substitute its view of the merits of an administrative decision... It remains a robust form of review” (para 13).

paragraphs.summary: Court explains reviewing courts must respect tribunal's reasoning and not substitute own reasons, but review is robust.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal in Singh confirmed reasonableness standard applies to admissibility of new evidence
propositions.quote: The Federal Court of Appeal in Singh confirmed that the reasonableness standard applies to decisions on the admissibility of new evidence (Singh para 29). Subsection 110(4) conditions are essential and must be met before considering other criteria like probative value or credibility (Singh para 35-36).

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision-maker confirmed reasonableness standard applies to admissibility of new evidence per Singh.

propositions.text: Section 110(4) IRPA requires new evidence to emerge after RPD decision, be unavailable before, or not reasonably presented
propositions.quote: According to section 110(4) of the IRPA, the RAD could only accept new evidence if: (a) it emerged after the RPD decision, (b) it was not reasonably available at the time of the decision, or (c) the applicant could not reasonably have been expected to present the evidence to the RPD before its decision.

propositions.text: RAD must consider credibility, relevance, newness, and materiality when admitting new evidence under s.110(4)
propositions.quote: In determining the admissibility of new evidence under subsection 110(4), the RAD must also have regard to the implicit considerations of admissibility with respect to its credibility, relevance, newness, and materiality (see Singh at paras 38-49 citing Raza at paras 13-15).

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision-maker states s.110(4) IRPA conditions for new evidence and RAD must consider credibility, relevance, newness, materiality.

propositions.text: RAD appeal is not opportunity to submit additional evidence to fix RPD vulnerabilities
propositions.quote: I pause here to note that an RAD appeal does not serve as an opportunity to submit additional evidence to address the vulnerabilities highlighted by the RPD (see: Firooznam v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 FC 571 at para 27 citing to Abdullahi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 260 at para 15).

propositions.text: Applicants submitted new evidence to bolster credible threat argument
propositions.quote: In this case, the Applicants submitted new evidence to bolster their argument that they faced a credible threat in India.

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision-maker states RAD appeal not for new evidence to fix RPD issues; Applicants submitted new evidence to bolster threat claim.

propositions.text: RAD analyzed new evidence and admitted only Indian Criminal Code passage; rejected others as could have been presented or lacked credibility
propositions.quote: In my view, the RAD undertook a detailed analysis of each new piece of evidence presented before it (see paras 23-36 of my reasons). It reasonably concluded that it would only admit the passage of the Indian Criminal Code (Exhibit H), because the remaining evidence either could have been put to the RPD, or the evidence was neither credible nor relevant.

propositions.text: No reviewable errors in RAD rejecting affidavits, letter, and medical certificate evidence
propositions.quote: I do not see any reviewable errors in how the RAD rejected the remaining evidence (i.e. the five undated affidavits signed by the Applicants’ neighbours (Exhibits A-E), the undated letter written by Jatinder Singh’s son (Exhibit F) and Jatinder Singh’s medical certificate (Exhibit G)).

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD reasonably admitted only Indian Criminal Code and properly rejected other evidence without reviewable errors.

propositions.text: RAD reasonably found undated affidavits with errors lacked credibility; errors not mere typos but serious
propositions.quote: It was reasonable for the RAD to conclude that the first five exhibits (i.e. the undated documents that had grammatical and spelling errors in the wet seals applied by a notary), lacked credibility. These were no mere typographical mistakes.

propositions.text: Official notary seal errors akin to misspelled government stamps on official documents per Mohamed
propositions.quote: The official seal of a notary is more akin to a misspelled government stamp placed on an allegedly official document (as was the case in Mohamed v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) at para 24).

propositions.text: Affidavits could have been presented to RPD as they concern pre-hearing events, so s.110(4) criteria not met
propositions.quote: Furthermore, with greater due diligence, these five affidavits could have been put before the RPD, as they contain information about events that occurred prior to the hearing. Consequently, this evidence doesn't meet the criteria in s. 110(4) as it could have been presented during the hearing.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD reasonably rejected undated affidavits with serious errors and that affidavits could have been presented earlier.

propositions.text: RAD reasonably found letter and medical certificate evidence inadmissible under s.110(4) as pre-hearing and lacking explanation
propositions.quote: The RAD reasonably concluded that the remaining evidence (i.e. Akashdeep Singh’s letter and Jatinder Singh’s medical certificate) failed to meet any of the criteria specified under section 110(4) of the IRPA. This evidence could have been submitted prior to the RPD hearing, as both exhibits pertain to pre-hearing events. There was no adequate explanation for the failure of due diligence.

propositions.text: Undated, unsworn letter and unrelated medical certificate lacked credibility and relevance
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the undated and unsworn typed letter, along with a medical certificate from an unrelated individual, were appropriately considered lacking in credibility and relevance.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD reasonably rejected letter and medical certificate as inadmissible, lacking explanation, credibility, and relevance.

propositions.text: Court not convinced RAD was unreasonable in finding new evidence inadmissible except Indian Criminal Code
propositions.quote: Therefore, I have not been convinced that the RAD was not reasonable in finding that the new evidence was inadmissible but for the reference to the Indian Criminal Code.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes RAD was reasonable in finding new evidence inadmissible except Indian Criminal Code.

propositions.text: Applicants chose not to raise procedural fairness issues on judicial review, so issue not before Court
propositions.quote: While the RAD did address the procedural fairness issues raised on appeal, the Applicants made a deliberate decision not to raise procedural fairness concerns on judicial review. Consequently, this issue is not currently before the Court.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes Applicants did not raise procedural fairness on review, so issue not before Court.

propositions.text: RAD reasonably found Principal Applicant lacked credibility based on inconsistencies and contradictions
propositions.quote: Given that the new evidence was found to be inadmissible by application of s. 110(4) and the Raza factors, the only issue to consider is whether the RAD was reasonable in concluding that the Principal Applicant lacked credibility. In my view, the RAD reasonably considered the Principal Applicant’s credibility based on the series of inconsistencies and contradictions in the record before it.

propositions.text: Applicants failed to show RAD's credibility decision was unreasonable
propositions.quote: The Applicants did not discharge their burden challenging the decision to show that it was unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD reasonably concluded Principal Applicant lacked credibility; Applicants failed to show unreasonableness.

propositions.text: RAD reasonably made adverse credibility finding due to unexplained identical photo and late mention of Gogi
propositions.quote: In particular, it was reasonable for the RAD to make an adverse credibility finding given the Principal Applicant’s inability to provide an explanation for how the photograph he submitted for his refugee protection claim was the same as the “warrant notice” issued by a local police station . Nor did the Principal Applicant provide a plausible explanation for why he had failed to mention that Gogi was present on the Sikh temple’s construction site until the moment he was questioned about it during the hearing before the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD reasonably made adverse credibility finding due to unexplained photo and late mention of Gogi.

propositions.text: RAD reasonably found credibility undermined by omission of leg fracture and rod injury contradicting earlier testimony
propositions.quote: It was also open for the RAD to find that the Principal Applicant’s credibility was undermined by him omitting the fact that he had suffered a leg fracture which required that a rod be implanted, the said rod being damaged as a result of the “torture”. This directly contradicted his earlier testimony concerning the injuries he had sustained.

propositions.text: Further injury shortly before departure unlikely to be forgotten
propositions.quote: Indeed, the further injury to the leg would have occurred in late April 2017, merely a few weeks before the Applicants’ departure to Canada. It is hard to see how such an event could have been forgotten.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD reasonably concluded credibility undermined by omission of leg injury shortly before departure.

propositions.text: Applicant must show serious shortcomings in decision to fail justification, intelligibility, and transparency per Vavilov
propositions.quote: An applicant must on judicial review satisfy the Court “that there are sufficiently serious shortcomings in the decision such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency” (Vavilov, para 100). The identified flaw must not be peripheral or superficial.

paragraphs.summary: Court states applicant must show serious shortcomings in decision to fail justification and transparency per Vavilov.

propositions.text: Credibility findings supported by contradictions, inconsistencies, omissions unless peripheral; administrative decision maker better positioned
propositions.quote: Lawani v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 924, usefully summarized principles applicable to the review of decisions made on the basis of the credibility of an applicant. Not only is the administrative decision maker better positioned to make assessments of testimonies, but an accumulation of contradictions, inconsistencies and omissions can support negative conclusions about the credibility of witnesses as long as the said flaws are not with respect to peripheral issues.

propositions.text: Searching for microscopic or peripheral issues may constitute reviewable errors
propositions.quote: An examination of a testimony in search of “microscopic” issues or peripheral issues might well constitute reviewable errors.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains credibility findings supported by contradictions unless peripheral; searching for minor issues may be error.

propositions.text: Credibility findings on critical claim elements can extend to the evidence as a whole, using common sense and rationality.
propositions.quote: credibility findings concerning important or critical elements of a claim can well extend to the evidence as a whole. Common sense and rationality are not excluded from the courtroom.

propositions.text: Conclusions on witness credibility may be based on implausibilities, common sense, and human experience.
propositions.quote: Conclusions may be reached about a witness’ credibility based on implausibilities, common sense and human experience.

propositions.text: Findings must be sensitive to cultural differences.
propositions.quote: I hasten to add that findings must be sensitive to cultural differences.

paragraphs.summary: The court states credibility findings can cover all evidence using common sense, implausibilities, and must respect cultural differences.

propositions.text: Contradictions, omissions, and implausibilities in this case were significant.
propositions.quote: The contradictions, omissions and, in effect, implausibilities in this case were significant.

propositions.text: Applicants failed to show shortcomings in the RAD decision that would make it unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The Applicants could not make a case that there were shortcomings in the RAD decision that could make the decision unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds significant contradictions and that applicants failed to prove the RAD decision was unreasonable.

propositions.text: The judicial review application is dismissed.
propositions.quote: The judicial review application is dismissed.

propositions.text: No serious question of general importance was submitted, so no question is certified by the Court.
propositions.quote: No serious question of general importance was submitted by the parties, and therefore no question is certified by the Court.

propositions.text: Judgment in IMM-4013-22 dismisses the judicial review application and denies certification under s 74 of IRPA.
propositions.quote: THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that: The judicial review application is dismissed. There is no question to be certified pursuant to s 74 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

propositions.text: The style of cause lists Sahib Singh et al as applicants and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration as respondent.
propositions.quote: STYLE OF CAUSE: SAHIB SINGH, JASWINDER KAUR, PARMEET KAUR, ARMAN SINGH v THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION

propositions.text: Hearing took place in Montréal, Quebec on March 15, 2023; judgment dated June 29, 2023 by Judge Roy.
propositions.quote: PLACE OF HEARING: Montréal, Quebec DATE OF HEARING: March 15, 2023 JUDGMENT AND REASONS: ROY J. DATED: june 29, 2023

propositions.text: Applicants represented by Miguel Mendez; respondent represented by Zoé Richard.
propositions.quote: APPEARANCES: Miguel Mendez For The Applicants Zoé Richard For The Respondent

propositions.text: Solicitors of record: Étude Légale Stewart Istvanffy for applicants; Attorney General of Canada for respondent.
propositions.quote: SOLICITORS OF RECORD: Étude Légale Stewart Istvanffy Barristers and Solicitors Montréal, Quebec For The Applicants Attorney General of Canada Montréal, Quebec For The Respondent

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the judicial review, denies certification, and records procedural facts including parties and counsel.
